title: Quanch Island
summary: Quanch is recorded as an island in Great South Bay opposite Bellport in Brookhaven. The name appears in a town-record description involving meadowland and Whale House Point.
map_geometry_source: Unverified former general point withdrawn 2026-09-24. Tooker pp. 201–202 and Shaw (1895), note to p. 41, establish regional context, not the former open-water coordinate.
history_content: The island is part of the Bellport and Great South Bay marsh-and-meadow landscape. The dated 1773 record is handled as a timeline entry with its source citation.
translation_content:
No separate translation is given for Quanch in the available references. The name is preserved as a recorded island placename in the Bellport bay landscape.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names always reflect the culture and the values and the priority of the people who have the power to make those place names stick.”

— Ruth Mostern, How Are Places Named in the US? (2025), quoted interview statement

Quanch Island keeps a smaller Great South Bay island and meadow name visible alongside better-known Bellport and Fire Island geography, preserving a local record of Indigenous naming in the coastal landscape.
preservation_content: Quanch Island keeps a smaller Great South Bay island and meadow name visible alongside better-known Bellport and Fire Island geography, preserving a local record of Indigenous naming in the coastal landscape.
whereintheworld_content:
Quanch belongs to the Bellport Bay and Fire Island historical landscape, but the precise island intended by the older boundary descriptions has not been established here. The former approximate pin in open Bellport Bay has been removed rather than presented as a verified island location.

Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island (1911), pp. 201–202, cites Brookhaven boundary records. Edward R. Shaw’s 1895 Legends of Fire Island Beach and the South Side, note to p. 41, describes Quanch as a landing on the beach opposite Otis’s Point. That description supplies regional context but does not establish an exact modern island coordinate. A reliable historic-map or survey match is needed before a pin is restored.
